analysis.one_liner: Lets banks, securities firms, and insurers merge into single financial holding companies, with community-lending and consumer protections attached.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate's top Democrat with 9 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Banking Committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tear down the Depression-era Glass-Steagall walls that kept banks, securities firms, and insurance companies separate, letting them combine into financial holding companies. Unlike the financial modernization law Congress actually passed later that year, this version would tie that freedom to conditions: banks had to be well capitalized, well managed, and hold at least a satisfactory community-lending (CRA) rating, with firewalls between insured deposits and riskier affiliates. It would also create a federal crime for obtaining customers' financial information by fraud, expand Federal Home Loan Bank affordable-housing subsidies, and fund training for low-income entrepreneurs.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks, securities firms, and insurers that want to combine and sell each other's products under one roof. Low- and moderate-income homebuyers would gain from expanded Federal Home Loan Bank affordable-housing subsidies, disadvantaged entrepreneurs from new microenterprise grants, and all bank customers from a new anti-fraud law covering financial information.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big financial firms; some low-income borrowers

how_it_helps.text: A bank holding company could only gain the new combined powers if all its insured banks were well capitalized, well managed, and had at least a satisfactory record of meeting community credit needs under the Community Reinvestment Act.
The bill would make it a federal civil and criminal violation, enforceable by the FTC, banking regulators, and states, to obtain a financial institution's customer information under false pretenses.

It would expand Federal Home Loan Bank affordable-housing programs to include direct subsidies (not just subsidized interest rates) and allow advances secured by small business, agricultural, and low-income community development loans.

It would create the PRIME Act, a grant program for nonprofits providing training and technical assistance to disadvantaged microentrepreneurs, including very low-income people and those on Indian reservations.
It would preserve state antitrust laws and a list of state insurance consumer protections, including rules against forcing borrowers to buy insurance from the bank as a condition of a loan.

analysis.who_pays: Large financial firms would bear the cost: Community Reinvestment Act conditions on every new expansion, capital firewalls between banks and their securities and insurance affiliates, functional regulation by the SEC and state insurance regulators, and limits on cross-marketing commercial products through banks. The public would also absorb whatever added risk comes from placing insured deposits inside larger, more complex conglomerates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large banks, insurers, and securities firms

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Glass-Steagall prohibitions would allow insured deposits to sit inside companies that underwrite securities and make merchant-banking investments, concentrating risk in bigger institutions; the bill's own firewalls and capital rules are the only buffer against that.

The bill would create wholesale financial institutions that can operate without deposit insurance and are subject to the Community Reinvestment Act only if they have an insured affiliate, letting some lenders escape community-lending obligations.

It would preempt state laws restricting affiliations among banks, insurers, and securities firms, and bar states from regulating banks' insurance activities in ways that treat banks worse than other insurance sellers, trimming state-level consumer safeguards.

It would sharply limit the Federal Reserve's authority over nonbank subsidiaries of financial holding companies, barring the Fed from imposing capital rules on subsidiaries that meet another regulator's standards and restricting examinations to cases showing material risk to an affiliated bank.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer side of this bill is real but secondary: the CRA condition, the financial-information fraud law, and the housing and microenterprise programs would genuinely help ordinary people. But the bill's center of gravity is allowing banks, securities firms, and insurers to merge, which concentrates financial power and concentrates risk around insured deposits. An honest supporter would concede that the deregulation is the price paid for the protections, that preemption of some state insurance rules gives back a layer of consumer protection, and that history showed financial conglomerates built on this structure amplified the 2008 crisis.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and was never scheduled for a hearing or a vote; it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle, the Senate Democratic leader, introduced the bill on March 25, 1999 for himself and nine other Democratic senators including Paul Sarbanes, Christopher Dodd, John Kerry, Charles Schumer, and John Edwards.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No hearing, committee markup, floor vote, or any other action was ever recorded on the bill for the remainder of the Congress.

Financial modernization did not wait for this bill: Congress passed a different version of Glass-Steagall repeal, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, in November 1999, without the CRA-linked structure and stronger privacy provisions this bill contained.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large financial conglomerates came out ahead. The industry got Glass-Steagall repeal that same year through the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, which carried weaker privacy protections and no requirement that conglomerate expansion be tied to satisfactory Community Reinvestment Act ratings — conditions this bill would have imposed. The consumers who would have gained from those conditions came out with less.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the bill never reached the floor, so no roll-call vote exists to show where Republicans stood.

industries.industry: Large bank, securities, and insurance conglomerates
industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to let banks, securities firms, and insurers affiliate by repealing Glass-Steagall sections 20 and 32 and creating financial holding companies. In exchange it conditions that expansion on strong capital, good management, and satisfactory community-lending ratings, and imposes firewalls and functional regulation, so the industry's gain runs partly alongside consumer protections.

industries.industry: Community banks (assets of $100 million or less)
industries.note: The bill concedes the need to study its projected impact on these institutions and expands Federal Home Loan Bank access for community financial institutions, but larger combined rivals would compete harder for their customers. Community banks losing ground to conglomerates is a loss ordinary depositors in small towns share.

industries.industry: State insurance regulators and independent insurance agents
industries.note: The bill preserves state regulation of the business of insurance and McCarran-Ferguson, but preempts state affiliation laws and bars states from regulating banks' insurance activities in ways that treat banks worse than other insurers. Independent agents would face banks selling insurance directly.

The bill creates a charter for wholesale financial institutions that need not carry deposit insurance and are subject to the Community Reinvestment Act only if they hold an insured affiliate, letting these lenders avoid community-lending obligations that apply to insured banks.

The bill would create the PRIME Act grant program funding training and technical assistance for disadvantaged entrepreneurs, with grants targeted in part to very low-income people including those on Indian reservations.
